facts.raw_span: A 55-year-old man underwent right hemicolectomy for moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon
staged as IIIB (T4N1M0)
He had no thrombophilic disorders
Preoperative carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and CA19-9 levels were normal
He completed six months of adjuvant chemotherapy
Thirteen months after surgery, follow-up CT revealed a 25 mm lesion in segment 8 of the liver
hepatitis B and C serologies were negative
Tumor markers including CEA, CA19-9, α-fetoprotein, and PIVKA-II were all within normal limits
CTA demonstrated a liver tumor with two components: a solid portion that enhanced in the early phase and washed out in the delayed phase, and a cystic component
CTAP showed absence of the right portal vein and a perfusion defect throughout the right lobe, suggestive of portal vein tumor thrombus
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography showed no communication with the biliary tree
bile cytology was negative for malignancy

concepts.why: The patient has a history of colorectal cancer and now presents with a liver lesion that has characteristics concerning for metastasis, including a solid and cystic component and portal vein tumor thrombus.
The liver tumor has a solid and cystic component and is associated with portal vein tumor thrombus, which are features that can be seen in hepatocellular carcinoma.
The liver tumor has a cystic component and is not communicating with the biliary tree, which could suggest an intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
It explains the liver lesion in a patient with a history of colorectal cancer.

rationales.F01: History of colorectal cancer increases likelihood of liver metastasis
rationales.F06: New liver lesion is suspicious for metastasis or primary liver cancer
rationales.F09: Liver tumor characteristics are consistent with metastasis or primary liver cancer
rationales.F10: Portal vein tumor thrombus is more commonly associated with liver metastasis from colorectal cancer

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's history of moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon and the presence of a liver tumor with characteristics consistent with metastasis, such as a solid portion that enhanced in the early phase and washed out in the delayed phase, support this diagnosis.
